messages.subject: Statistical power and significance in an imperfect dataset with a limited number of sites
messages.subject_clean: Statistical power and significance in an imperfect dataset with a limited number of sites
messages.body_plain:
James Shelley
Sep 21, 2023, 9:30:11 PM



to unmarked
Hi team,

First of all, thank you for this package and your continuous support.

My question relates to an analysis of a long-term fish observation database which I'm considering publishing. I am after a sense check of my conclusions/assumptions before I commit to preparing a manuscript- one probably aimed at a modest journal (~IF 2) and maybe in the form of a short communication.

I have database that includes 42 years of data collected over the management area of a large city that has 5 major drainage areas. Think of it a bit like a citizen science database. Sampling was not spatially or temporally consistent across sites within river basins, so I've split the river basins up into sub-catchment areas which act as my 'sites' and I've combined all observations within each site for each year. To reduce the amount of missing data, my sites are fairly large and relatively few (32 sites total, see figure below for example). In the dynamic occupancy model I am using each year of data as secondary surveys (replicates) and three years are combined to make one primary sampling occasion (14 primary sampling occasions over 42 years).
The single species I'm interested is migratory, swimming to and from the ocean each year. Historically, barriers to migration have impeded their upstream migration at several locations, restricting their distribution. Efforts have been made to remove these barriers over the last couple of decades though and the expectation is that these species have benefited through an increase in distribution. My aim is to test this assumption.

The dataset is imperfect, so I've kept the model simple with one explanatory variable that describes the proportion of a catchment (at the point where a site is) that is unimpeded by barriers in each year. As we move towards the present, this proportion has increased.

The results show that the distribution of the target species has more than doubled over the study period. The CIs don't overlap between the first and last seasons, indicating that the change is significant. Large jumps in occupancy are observed when various barriers are removed. Furthermore, colonisation is significantly correlated with the 'barrier removal' variable. I've compared the model versus a null model and other variations to show that it describes the data best. For the best model P-hat = 0.96. chi-squ = 0.083.

The results fit expectations, are significant, and the model passes the model fit test. That said, I'm working with 32 sites and a fair bit of missing data and the power to detect change is low. I had a play around with the power analysis presented in Guillera‐Arroita, G., & Lahoz‐Monfort, J. J. (2012), which suggested I'd need 2-3x more sites to achieve power of 0.8. I think the CIs from the occupancy analysis might be a reasonable guide as to the power of the analysis given my actual dataset though?

I was hoping you could provide your general take on the validity of the findings. Does the poor site replication mean that the results are effectively unreliable, or do the various tests of significance and model fit indicate that it is reliable enough?

The whole thing is rough around the edges, but I think it could be a worthwhile example of the benefit of mining a historic dataset to assess the impact of waterway management efforts that have been taking place over far longer time periods than any standardised monitoring programs capture.

## This is the model used
dynamic_occ_m1 <- colext(
  # Psi depends on initial proportion of catchment available
  psiformula = ~Barrier1,
  # colonization depends on change the proportion of catchment available
  gammaformula = ~barriers_time,
  # extinction depends on the proportion of catchment available
  epsilonformula = ~barriers_time  ,
  # Detection varies between years
  pformula = ~year,
  #
  data = Tupong_unmarkedMultFrame,
  method = "BFGS")

Thanks in advance for your time. It's much appreciated.

Regards,
James

messages.body_plain:
hi James,
 From what I understand here you are testing a covariate that varies by site and year, so you have actually quite a bit more information to make this test than just the 32 sites. When you said you played around with the Guillera-Arroita and Lahoz-Monfort power analysis, it's not clear whether the model for that was consistent with the actual model you're using. If not, you should just repeat the power analysis for your exact model for a better assessment of your specific design.
regards
andy

messages.subject: Simulating data for a multi-method project
messages.subject_clean: Simulating data for a multi-method project
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have run into a bit of a snag while trying to simulate data to consider my analysis + hypotheses for a project. Specifically, I would like to assess data on amphibian diseases using a single season multi-scale (or multi-method) occupancy model. I have 24 sites that I visited 3 times in a season; during each visit I collected skin swabs from ~12 individuals and  each swab is tested in triplicate in the lab. In this case we are treating each test as analogous to a survey, and each individual could be thought of as the "subsite". Thus my simulated data should be a 24*108 matrix.

I have followed the documentation on the simulate() function, but instead of using occu() I am using goccu(). I want to simulate an effect of temperature on occupancy. However, when I tryo to run the simulate() function I get the error argument "psiformula" is missing, with no default.I'm guessing this error is because I am not specifying the formula correctly, but I haven't seen any documentation on how to use simulate() and goccu() together. I would appreciate any help clarifying this issue, and have copied my current code below.

library(unmarked)
set.seed(1234)
ponds <- 24 #number of sites
frogs <- 12 #number of frogs PER VISIT
visits <- 3 #number of visits to each site
tests <- 3 #number of tests per frog
total_frogs <- frogs*visits
total_tests <- frogs*visits*tests #total number of tests for each pond for the season

# Create an empty dataframe for the detection data
det <- matrix(NA, nrow = ponds, ncol = total_tests)

# Create a site lvl covar
site_covs <- data.frame(temp = rnorm(ponds))

umf <- unmarkedFrameGOccu(y = det, siteCovs = site_covs, numPrimary = total_frogs)
head(umf)
formula <- ~1~1~temp
simulate(umf, model = goccu, formula = formula)
--
Reed Scott (he/him/his)
Email: rscot...@gmail.com
Phone: 716-381-1467

messages.body_plain:
Hi Reed,

You need to provide the same arguments to simulate() that you would provide to goccu() when actually fitting the model. So in this case instead of 'formula' you'd provide separate 'psiformula' , 'phiformula', and 'pformula' arguments to simulate (see ?goccu).

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andy,

Good questions. I've revisited the power analysis. I'd appreciate it if you could review whether it accurately captures my model.

In my model, three years (3 repeat visits) constitute a 'season' and the barrier covariate changes between seasons only. I have data for 42 repeat visits within 14 seasons for which I am estimating changes in occupancy.

The detection history looks like this for each site 001 101 000 110 111 010 001 110 000 101 111 001 101 010

# power of the design using the closed formula
S <- 32 # number of sites
K <- 3 # number of replicates (I believe in each season and not overall?)
R <- 1.0 # proportional change in occupancy (estimated occupancy doubled)
psi1 <- 0.42       # initial occupancy probability
p <- 0.5 # detection probability
alpha <-0.05 # significance level

(powerF <- calcPowerFormula(S1=S,S2=S,K1=K,K2=K,p1=p,p2=p,psi1,R,alpha))

This actually suggest that there is high power 0.98.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Reed,

The way goccu calculates the likelihood requires a list of all the possible true availability states for a given site. So for example if you have two primary periods, the possible availability states are 0-0 (if the species was not available in either primary period), 1-0 (avialable for first and not for second), 0-1, 1-1. If you have three periods it's 0-0-0, 1-0-0, and so on.

There are always 2^T states where T is the number of primary periods. In your code you specified 36 primary periods which is 2^36 = something like 6.8 x 10^10 possible states. R can't handle this. This implies there is a practical upper limit to the number of primary periods goccu can handle (much like there is a practical limit to the number of species occuMulti can handle).

There may be some other way to calculate the likelihood that avoids this issue, but I'm not aware of it. Maybe someone on the listserv knows. Fitting the model in a Bayesian framework might work.

Looking at your simulation setup it seems like you actually have three levels of repeated samples within a site: frogs, visits, and tests. I'm not sure what these represent exactly, but I think this is one more level of organization than goccu can handle. It can only handle two levels: primary periods, and secondary periods within primary periods.

Ken

Hi Ken,

Thanks for the explanation. That makes a lot of sense and actually helps me a lot! I can do work on a smaller simulated dataset. I will have to consider how I want to approach the fact that it won't be able to handle as many tests as I have, but that might be a better question for the HMEcology listserv.

To clarify, visits aren't really considered in the structure of the data; they're just used to determine how many frogs (and how many tests) are collected total across the season. If I wanted to, I could consider them as part of the model and do a dynamic multiscale occupancy model, but that's not something I'm interested in at the moment.

Thanks again Ken, I really appreciate your help.
-Reed

> Hi Andy,
>
> Good questions. I've revisited the power analysis. I'd appreciate it if you could review whether it accurately captures my model.
>
> In my model, three years (3 repeat visits) constitute a 'season' and the barrier covariate changes between seasons only. I have data for 42 repeat visits within 14 seasons for which I am estimating changes in occupancy.
>
> The detection history looks like this for each site 001 101 000 110 111 010 001 110 000 101 111 001 101 010
>
> # power of the design using the closed formula
> S <- 32 # number of sites
> K <- 3 # number of replicates (I believe in each season and not overall?)
> R <- 1.0 # proportional change in occupancy (estimated occupancy doubled)
> psi1 <- 0.42       # initial occupancy probability
> p <- 0.5 # detection probability
> alpha <-0.05 # significance level
>
> (powerF <- calcPowerFormula(S1=S,S2=S,K1=K,K2=K,p1=p,p2=p,psi1,R,alpha))
>
> This actually suggest that there is high power 0.98.

When you said you played around with the Guillera-Arroita and Lahoz-Monfort power analysis, it's not clear whether the model for that was consistent with the actual model you're using. If not, you should just repeat the power analysis for your exact model for a better assessment of your specific design.
> > regards
> > andy
> >
> >
> > On Sat, Feb 1, 2025 at 7:29 PM James Shelley <jamessh...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > 

> > > to unmarked
> > > Hi team,
> > >
> > > First of all, thank you for this package and your continuous support.
> > >
> > > My question relates to an analysis of a long-term fish observation database which I'm considering publishing. I am after a sense check of my conclusions/assumptions before I commit to preparing a manuscript- one probably aimed at a modest journal (~IF 2) and maybe in the form of a short communication.
> > >
> > > I have database that includes 42 years of data collected over the management area of a large city that has 5 major drainage areas. Think of it a bit like a citizen science database. Sampling was not spatially or temporally consistent across sites within river basins, so I've split the river basins up into sub-catchment areas which act as my 'sites' and I've combined all observations within each site for each year. To reduce the amount of missing data, my sites are fairly large and relatively few (32 sites total, see figure below for example). In the dynamic occupancy model I am using each year of data as secondary surveys (replicates) and three years are combined to make one primary sampling occasion (14 primary sampling occasions over 42 years).
> > > The single species I'm interested is migratory, swimming to and from the ocean each year. Historically, barriers to migration have impeded their upstream migration at several locations, restricting their distribution. Efforts have been made to remove these barriers over the last couple of decades though and the expectation is that these species have benefited through an increase in distribution. My aim is to test this assumption.
> > >
> > > The dataset is imperfect, so I've kept the model simple with one explanatory variable that describes the proportion of a catchment (at the point where a site is) that is unimpeded by barriers in each year. As we move towards the present, this proportion has increased.
> > >
> > > The results show that the distribution of the target species has more than doubled over the study period. The CIs don't overlap between the first and last seasons, indicating that the change is significant. Large jumps in occupancy are observed when various barriers are removed. Furthermore, colonisation is significantly correlated with the 'barrier removal' variable. I've compared the model versus a null model and other variations to show that it describes the data best. For the best model P-hat = 0.96. chi-squ = 0.083.
> > >
> > > The results fit expectations, are significant, and the model passes the model fit test. That said, I'm working with 32 sites and a fair bit of missing data and the power to detect change is low. I had a play around with the power analysis presented in Guillera‐Arroita, G., & Lahoz‐Monfort, J. J. (2012), which suggested I'd need 2-3x more sites to achieve power of 0.8. I think the CIs from the occupancy analysis might be a reasonable guide as to the power of the analysis given my actual dataset though?
> > >
> > > I was hoping you could provide your general take on the validity of the findings. Does the poor site replication mean that the results are effectively unreliable, or do the various tests of significance and model fit indicate that it is reliable enough?
> > >
> > > The whole thing is rough around the edges, but I think it could be a worthwhile example of the benefit of mining a historic dataset to assess the impact of waterway management efforts that have been taking place over far longer time periods than any standardised monitoring programs capture.
> > >
> > > ## This is the model used
> > > dynamic_occ_m1 <- colext(
> > >   # Psi depends on initial proportion of catchment available
> > >   psiformula = ~Barrier1,
> > >   # colonization depends on change the proportion of catchment available
> > >   gammaformula = ~barriers_time,
> > >   # extinction depends on the proportion of catchment available
> > >   epsilonformula = ~barriers_time  ,
> > >   # Detection varies between years
> > >   pformula = ~year,
> > >   #
> > >   data = Tupong_unmarkedMultFrame,
> > >   method = "BFGS")
> > >
> > > Thanks in advance for your time. It's much appreciated.
> > >
> > > Regards,

messages.body_plain:
Hi James,

I am a bit concerned with the way you've set up your replicates. If three years is a single 'season' then you are assuming that the fish population is closed at a site over any three-year period. Is that realistic in your system? If the occupancy is known to be changing over time it would seem to me that it could change within a 3-year period, and thus you can't really estimate detection probability.

Second, I am not that familiar with the Guillera-Arroita/Lahoz-Monfort power analysis approach, but it looks to me like their formula is meant to detect differences in single-season occupancy between two independent sets of sites. They do mention on page 862 the case where the same sites are sampled in two different seasons and ways of handling that. But this seems different to me than a power analysis for specifically a dynamic occupancy model, where you also have to estimate other parameters like colonization and extinction.

I am not exactly sure what calcPowerFormula() function is doing (or where it's from) but I suspect what you are calculating there is your power to detect a doubling of (single-season) occupancy from one set of sites (presumably your 32 sites in "season" 1) compared to a second set of sites (your 32 sites in the final "season", which are assumed to be independent).

One final caution: it's not clear why you chose R = 1 specifically, but hopefully it is not based on an effect size from one of your actual fitted models, since post-hoc power tests are not generally useful.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Thanks guys.

I've addressed both Ken and Andy's comments below.

The species is diadromous, the adults stay in a stream at a given site, while the newly hatched larvae drift downstream to the ocean. The adult population at a given site can be considered closed.

I am quite sure the power analysis relates to comparisons between sites or time periods... for instance, it is stated in the abstract "We demonstrate that our results and discussion are applicable regardless of whether independence or Markovian dependence is assumed in the occupancy status of sites between seasons, and illustrate their utility when designing to detect a trend in multiple-season studies."

Yes, I am calculating the power to detect a doubling of (single-season) occupancy from one set of sites (presumably your 32 sites in "season" 1) compared to a second set of sites (your 32 sites in the final "season", which are assumed to be independent). I believe you are correct regarding what the calcPowerFormula() is doing. I'm most interested in a change in occupancy between the first and last season, so I thought this approach achieves that.

I am analysing a historic public dataset retrospectively, and I set K=1 (a doubling in occupancy) based on the results of the colext estimates because I'd like to know if I can reliably interpret the significance of the results given the dataset. I intend on using the results of a power analysis and an interpretation of the confidence intervals to provide insight into this.

I'm keen to try the unmarked power analysis if it has been extended to cover muli-season models, but that vignet focusses on single-season models and when I try to run a colext model I get the warning " Error: model argument must be occu, occuRN, or occuPEN". Is there an updated vignet?

Regards,
James

messages.body_plain:
Thanks guys.

I've addressed both Ken and Andy's comments below.

The species is diadromous, the adults stay in a stream at a given site, while the newly hatched larvae drift downstream to the ocean. The adult population at a given site can be considered closed.

I am quite sure the power analysis relates to comparisons between sites or time periods... for instance, it is stated in the abstract "We demonstrate that our results and discussion are applicable regardless of whether independence or Markovian dependence is assumed in the occupancy status of sites between seasons, and illustrate their utility when designing to detect a trend in multiple-season studies."

Yes, I am calculating the power to detect a doubling of (single-season) occupancy from one set of sites (presumably your 32 sites in "season" 1) compared to a second set of sites (your 32 sites in the final "season", which are assumed to be independent). I believe you are correct regarding what the calcPowerFormula() is doing. I'm most interested in a change in occupancy between the first and last season, so I thought this approach achieves that.

I am analysing a historic public dataset retrospectively, and I set K=1 (a doubling in occupancy) based on the results of the colext estimates because I'd like to know if I can reliably interpret the significance of the results given the dataset. I intend on using the results of a power analysis and an interpretation of the confidence intervals to provide insight into this.

I'll have a go at the unmarked power analysis- thanks.

Regards,
James

messages.body_plain:
Post-hoc power analysis won't tell you anything beyond what you already know from the p-value in the fitted model. If you fit a model, estimate an effect size that has a significant p-value, then run a power analysis on that effect size, you'll always appear to have high power. Same thing for the opposite - if you find a small effect size with a corresponding large p-value, the power analysis will always tell you you have low power. In both cases you won't learn anything about the actual power for the design.

For power analysis output to tell you something useful you should hypothesize possible effect size(s) before collecting (or in your case before analyzing) the data.

See https://library.virginia.edu/data/articles/post-hoc-power-calculations-are-not-useful for a discussion of this and simulation (with t-tests, but the principle is the same).

Below is a demo of how to use powerAnalysis() with colext. Based on your question (testing for a change in occupancy between year 1 and year 14) I think the dynamic occupancy model may not be what you want. The dynamic model only estimates occupancy parameters for the initial occupancy state - there is no way to include a parameter in the model that explicitly tests for a change in occupancy over time. It might work better to use a 'stacked' model where your sites are actually site-years, and you include a covariate for year which would directly address your question. Of course, stacked models have their own issues which have been thoroughly discussed on the listserv.

-------------------------

library(unmarked)

# Study design
N <- 32
T <- 14
J <- 3

# Create blank unmarkedMultFrame (used by colext)
y <- matrix(NA, nrow=N, ncol=T*J)
temp <- rnorm(N) # fake site covariate for example
umf <- unmarkedMultFrame(y=y, siteCovs=data.frame(temp=temp), numPrimary=T)

# Run the model without effect sizes in order to
# see how the effect sizes should be structured
# Note we need to specify the same formula argumenst as colext()
# We want a temp effect on initial occ so we set psiformula ~temp
powerAnalysis(umf, psiformula=~temp, gammaformula=~1, epsilonformula=~1,
              pformula=~1)

# Match the structure provided
ef <- list(psi = c(0, -0.5), # negative effect of temp on initial occ
           col = 0,
           ext = 0,
           det = 0) # other parameters set at 0.5 (0 on logit scale)

# Actually run the analysis
pa <- powerAnalysis(umf, psiformula=~temp, gammaformula=~1, epsilonformula=~1,
                    pformula=~1, effects = ef)

# Low power to detect effect of temp effect size of -0.5
summary(pa, showIntercepts=TRUE)

> > The way goccu calculates the likelihood requires a list of all the possible true availability states for a given site. So for example if you have two primary periods, the possible availability states are 0-0 (if the species was not available in either primary period), 1-0 (avialable for first and not for second), 0-1, 1-1. If you have three periods it's 0-0-0, 1-0-0, and so on.
> >
> > There are always 2^T states where T is the number of primary periods. In your code you specified 36 primary periods which is 2^36 = something like 6.8 x 10^10 possible states. R can't handle this. This implies there is a practical upper limit to the number of primary periods goccu can handle (much like there is a practical limit to the number of species occuMulti can handle).
> >
> > There may be some other way to calculate the likelihood that avoids this issue, but I'm not aware of it. Maybe someone on the listserv knows. Fitting the model in a Bayesian framework might work.
> >
> > Looking at your simulation setup it seems like you actually have three levels of repeated samples within a site: frogs, visits, and tests. I'm not sure what these represent exactly, but I think this is one more level of organization than goccu can handle. It can only handle two levels: primary periods, and secondary periods within primary periods.

messages.body_plain:
simulate() should return an unmarkedFrame object (i.e., a dataset), or a list of such datasets, not a fitted model. So class(sim) should be a list of unmarkedFrames or a single unmarkedFrame.

In order to use predict, you'd need to take the simulated dataset and fit a model to it using goccu(), and then use predict on the fitted model. Have you done that extra step? It's not clear from your email/code. It might be helpful if you paste your complete code from start to finish where the error happens.

Hi Ken,

Sorry, I realized after I sent that exactly the point that you made. To clarify, I simulated a dataset where phi ~ betadiv. I then wanted to predict along a gradient of betadiv values the estimate of phi. I have included a full snippet of code below.

set.seed(1234)
ponds <- 24 #number of sites

frogs <- 2 #number of frogs PER VISIT

visits <- 3 #number of visits to each site
tests <- 3 #number of tests per frog
total_frogs <- frogs*visits
total_tests <- frogs*visits*tests #total number of tests for each pond for the season

# Create an empty dataframe for the detection data
det <- matrix(NA, nrow = ponds, ncol = total_tests)

# Create a site lvl covar

site_covs <- data.frame(temp = rnorm(ponds),betadiv = rnorm(ponds))

umf <- unmarkedFrameGOccu(y = det, siteCovs = site_covs, numPrimary = total_frogs)
head(umf)

simulate(umf, model = goccu,  psiformula = ~temp, phiformula =~ betadiv, pformula =~ 1)
coeff <- list(psi = c(0,-0.7),
                  phi = c(0,-0.7),
                  det = 0)

sim <- simulate(umf, model = goccu,  psiformula = ~temp, phiformula = ~betadiv, pformula =~ 1, coefs = coeff)

head(sim[[1]])
tempXpsiphiXbeta <- goccu(psiformula = ~temp, phiformula = ~betadiv, pformula =~ 1, data = sim[[1]])
summary(tempXpsiphiXbeta)
betadiv <- data.frame(betadiv = seq(from = -2, to = 2, by = 0.1))
betapredict <- unmarked::predict(tempXpsiphiXbeta, type = "phi", newdata = betadiv, appendData = T)

> > > > >> The way goccu calculates the likelihood requires a list of all the

> > > > >> have two primary periods, the possible availability states are 0-0
> > > (if the
> > > > >> species was not available in either primary period), 1-0 (avialable
> > > for
> > > > >> first and not for second), 0-1, 1-1. If you have three periods it's
> > > 0-0-0,
> > > > >> 1-0-0, and so on.
> > > > >>
> > > > >> There are always 2^T states where T is the number of primary periods.
> > > In
> > > > >> your code you specified 36 primary periods which is 2^36 = something
> > > like
> > > > >> 6.8 x 10^10 possible states. R can't handle this. This implies there

Your code works fine for me and outputs predictions. I wonder if there's just some predict method name collision issue in your R environment? I'd suggest first double checking you are on the most recent unmarked version (1.4.3) and then start a completely fresh R session with no other packages loaded, and run your code, and it should work.

> > > > for

> > > > like

Hi Ken,

I did as you suggested and still have the same error. I am running the most recent version of unmarked. I even updated RStudio just to be safe and still have the same problem. Any other suggestions?

-Reed

On Wed, Feb 5, 2025 at 1:52 PM Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com> wrote:

> Thanks, that's helpful.
>
> Your code works fine for me and outputs predictions. I wonder if there's just some predict method name collision issue in your R environment? I'd suggest first double checking you are on the most recent unmarked version (1.4.3) and then start a completely fresh R session with no other packages loaded, and run your code, and it should work.
>
> On Wed, Feb 05, 2025 at 01:33:38PM -0500, Reed Scott wrote:
> > Hi Ken,
> >
> > Sorry, I realized after I sent that exactly the point that you made. To
> > clarify, I simulated a dataset where phi ~ betadiv. I then wanted to
> > predict along a gradient of betadiv values the estimate of phi. I have
> > included a full snippet of code below.
> >
> > set.seed(1234)
> > ponds <- 24 #number of sites
> > frogs <- 2 #number of frogs PER VISIT
> > visits <- 3 #number of visits to each site
> > tests <- 3 #number of tests per frog
> > total_frogs <- frogs*visits
> > total_tests <- frogs*visits*tests #total number of tests for each pond for
> > the season
> >
> > # Create an empty dataframe for the detection data
> > det <- matrix(NA, nrow = ponds, ncol = total_tests)
> >
> > # Create a site lvl covar
> > site_covs <- data.frame(temp = rnorm(ponds),betadiv = rnorm(ponds))
> >
> > umf <- unmarkedFrameGOccu(y = det, siteCovs = site_covs, numPrimary =
> > total_frogs)
> > head(umf)
> > simulate(umf, model = goccu,  psiformula = ~temp, phiformula =~ betadiv,
> > pformula =~ 1)
> > coeff <- list(psi = c(0,-0.7),
> >                   phi = c(0,-0.7),
> >                   det = 0)
> > sim <- simulate(umf, model = goccu,  psiformula = ~temp, phiformula =
> > ~betadiv, pformula =~ 1, coefs = coeff)
> > head(sim[[1]])
> > tempXpsiphiXbeta <- goccu(psiformula = ~temp, phiformula = ~betadiv,
> > pformula =~ 1, data = sim[[1]])
> > summary(tempXpsiphiXbeta)
> > betadiv <- data.frame(betadiv = seq(from = -2, to = 2, by = 0.1))
> > betapredict <- unmarked::predict(tempXpsiphiXbeta, type = "phi", newdata =
> > betadiv, appendData = T)
> >
> > On Wed, Feb 5, 2025 at 12:56 PM Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com> wrote:
> >
> > > simulate() should return an unmarkedFrame object (i.e., a dataset), or a
> > > list of such datasets, not a fitted model. So class(sim) should be a list
> > > of unmarkedFrames or a single unmarkedFrame.
> > >
> > > In order to use predict, you'd need to take the simulated dataset and fit
> > > a model to it using goccu(), and then use predict on the fitted model. Have
> > > you done that extra step? It's not clear from your email/code. It might be
> > > helpful if you paste your complete code from start to finish where the
> > > error happens.
> > >
> > > On Wed, Feb 05, 2025 at 12:49:12PM -0500, Reed Scott wrote:
> > > > Hi Ken,
> > > >
> > > > tempXpsiphiXbeta is the output from a call to simulate data using goccu.
> > > > The class of the output is below. Additionally, I simulate the code using
> > > > this line: sim <- simulate(umf, model = goccu,  psiformula = ~temp,
> > > > phiformula = ~betadiv, pformula =~ 1, coefs = coeff)

> > > > > call to goccu()?

> > > > > > >> The way goccu calculates the likelihood requires a list of all the
> > > > > > >> possible true availability states for a given site. So for
> > > example if
> > > > > you
> > > > > > >> have two primary periods, the possible availability states are 0-0
> > > > > (if the
> > > > > > >> species was not available in either primary period), 1-0
> > > (avialable
> > > > > for
> > > > > > >> first and not for second), 0-1, 1-1. If you have three periods
> > > it's
> > > > > 0-0-0,
> > > > > > >> 1-0-0, and so on.
> > > > > > >>
> > > > > > >> There are always 2^T states where T is the number of primary
> > > periods.
> > > > > In
> > > > > > >> your code you specified 36 primary periods which is 2^36 =
> > > something
> > > > > like
> > > > > > >> 6.8 x 10^10 possible states. R can't handle this. This implies

> > > > > is a
> > > > > > >> practical upper limit to the number of primary periods goccu can

> > > > > of

> > > > > primary
> > > > > > >> periods, and secondary periods within primary periods.

> > > > Hi Ken,

> > > > Sorry, I realized after I sent that exactly the point that you made. To
> > > > clarify, I simulated a dataset where phi ~ betadiv. I then wanted to
> > > > predict along a gradient of betadiv values the estimate of phi. I have
> > > > included a full snippet of code below.
> > > >
> > > > set.seed(1234)
> > > > ponds <- 24 #number of sites
> > > > frogs <- 2 #number of frogs PER VISIT
> > > > visits <- 3 #number of visits to each site
> > > > tests <- 3 #number of tests per frog
> > > > total_frogs <- frogs*visits
> > > > total_tests <- frogs*visits*tests #total number of tests for each pond
> > > for
> > > > the season
> > > >
> > > > # Create an empty dataframe for the detection data
> > > > det <- matrix(NA, nrow = ponds, ncol = total_tests)
> > > >
> > > > # Create a site lvl covar
> > > > site_covs <- data.frame(temp = rnorm(ponds),betadiv = rnorm(ponds))
> > > >
> > > > umf <- unmarkedFrameGOccu(y = det, siteCovs = site_covs, numPrimary =
> > > > total_frogs)
> > > > head(umf)
> > > > simulate(umf, model = goccu,  psiformula = ~temp, phiformula =~ betadiv,
> > > > pformula =~ 1)
> > > > coeff <- list(psi = c(0,-0.7),
> > > >                   phi = c(0,-0.7),
> > > >                   det = 0)
> > > > sim <- simulate(umf, model = goccu,  psiformula = ~temp, phiformula =
> > > > ~betadiv, pformula =~ 1, coefs = coeff)
> > > > head(sim[[1]])
> > > > tempXpsiphiXbeta <- goccu(psiformula = ~temp, phiformula = ~betadiv,
> > > > pformula =~ 1, data = sim[[1]])
> > > > summary(tempXpsiphiXbeta)
> > > > betadiv <- data.frame(betadiv = seq(from = -2, to = 2, by = 0.1))
> > > > betapredict <- unmarked::predict(tempXpsiphiXbeta, type = "phi", newdata
> > > =
> > > > betadiv, appendData = T)
> > > >
> > > > On Wed, Feb 5, 2025 at 12:56 PM Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com>
> > > wrote:
> > > >
> > > > > simulate() should return an unmarkedFrame object (i.e., a dataset), or
> > > a
> > > > > list of such datasets, not a fitted model. So class(sim) should be a
> > > list
> > > > > of unmarkedFrames or a single unmarkedFrame.
> > > > >
> > > > > In order to use predict, you'd need to take the simulated dataset and
> > > fit
> > > > > a model to it using goccu(), and then use predict on the fitted model.
> > > Have
> > > > > you done that extra step? It's not clear from your email/code. It
> > > might be
> > > > > helpful if you paste your complete code from start to finish where the
> > > > > error happens.
> > > > >
> > > > > On Wed, Feb 05, 2025 at 12:49:12PM -0500, Reed Scott wrote:
> > > > > > Hi Ken,
> > > > > >

> > > > > > > > >> Hi Reed,
> > > > > > > > >>
> > > > > > > > >> The way goccu calculates the likelihood requires a list of
> > > all the
> > > > > > > > >> possible true availability states for a given site. So for
> > > > > example if
> > > > > > > you
> > > > > > > > >> have two primary periods, the possible availability states
> > > are 0-0
> > > > > > > (if the
> > > > > > > > >> species was not available in either primary period), 1-0
> > > > > (avialable
> > > > > > > for
> > > > > > > > >> first and not for second), 0-1, 1-1. If you have three periods
> > > > > it's
> > > > > > > 0-0-0,
> > > > > > > > >> 1-0-0, and so on.
> > > > > > > > >>
> > > > > > > > >> There are always 2^T states where T is the number of primary
> > > > > periods.
> > > > > > > In
> > > > > > > > >> your code you specified 36 primary periods which is 2^36 =
> > > > > something
> > > > > > > like
> > > > > > > > >> 6.8 x 10^10 possible states. R can't handle this. This implies
> > > > > there
> > > > > > > is a
> > > > > > > > >> practical upper limit to the number of primary periods goccu
> > > can
> > > > > > > handle
> > > > > > > > >> (much like there is a practical limit to the number of species
> > > > > > > occuMulti
> > > > > > > > >> can handle).
> > > > > > > > >>
> > > > > > > > >> There may be some other way to calculate the likelihood that
> > > > > avoids
> > > > > > > this
> > > > > > > > >> issue, but I'm not aware of it. Maybe someone on the listserv
> > > > > knows.

> > > > > > > > >>
> > > > > > > > >> Looking at your simulation setup it seems like you actually
> > > have
> > > > > three
> > > > > > > > >> levels of repeated samples within a site: frogs, visits, and
> > > > > tests.
> > > > > > > I'm not
> > > > > > > > >> sure what these represent exactly, but I think this is one
> > > more
> > > > > level
> > > > > > > of
> > > > > > > > >> organization than goccu can handle. It can only handle two
> > > levels:
> > > > > > > primary
> > > > > > > > >> periods, and secondary periods within primary periods.
> > > > > > > > >>
> > > > > > > > >> Ken

messages.subject: goccu - removal design - missing data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm having trouble replicating a multi-scale occupancy model in RMark using the goccu model.

The data are from the larksparrow example in the RMark documentation and features 2 sources of missing data.

The first source of missing data is imposed by a removal design with missing data for subsequent occasions after initial detection, and the second source of missing data is from a missing primary occasions at some sites.

I investigated behavior of the goccu model by imposing the removal design to the example dataset with NA for subsequent occasions after initial detection, and that worked well.  I'm thinking the problem involves missing primary occasions (subsamples) coded as NA.  The estimates of availability seem way to low when primary occasions are missing

I know MARK omits probability arguments for missing data from the likelihood, which appropriately estimates parameters for observed encounter histories.

Has anyone encountered problems with missing data for primary occasion in the goccu mode?

Any help on this is greatly appreciated.

David

I am working with the goccu function for a multi-scale model. I have 3 covariates for site occupancy, 4 for availability, and for 4 for detection. I don't want to explore any additive or interactive models for now.

I was thinking of using the dredge function but hesitate for two reasons: 1) I'm not sure if it supports unmarkedFitGOccu objects and 2) Based on some reading of prior posts it seems that whether dredging is advisable is questionable.

I'm wondering if there's any quick way to create the model set I'm trying to compare, or if I just need to create each model individually?

If it will help I'm happy to go in to my specific hypotheses.

-Reed

messages.body_plain:
I believe I have fixed the issue now in the dev version of the package. You can install it like this -

remotes::install_github("biodiverse/unmarked")

I'm now getting results that match both RMark and JAGS with the larksparrow data. If you are able to confirm this on your system, that would be helpful.

The patch is here:

https://github.com/biodiverse/unmarked/commit/a987357514c7acddc6e23410c01a96b49d053850

The missing primary periods were being skipped, but the likelihood was always using the full possible set of 2^T availability states instead of skipping the states that were not possible due to the missing primary periods. Those states are now properly dropped.

Ken

It turns-out I had an outdated version of Rtools, now updated, I can access the dev version using  remotes::install_github.

As you found, I am also recovering identical parameter estimates from the RMark example.

I am working with ornithology students, some of which have Mac OS.  The unmarked implementation of the model avoids problematic installation of MARK, so that will be great for the class.

Thanks for all your help!

David

messages.subject: occu() with unequal occasion length
messages.body_plain:
Dear Ken,

I am helping some colleagues who have a survey of long-eared owls with three occasions of unequal length (2, 2.5 and 5 mins or something). We want to do occupancy modeling and it would be good to account for this unequal occasion length. I know now how to specify the likelihood in R and could adapt that for unequal length. But before I do that I was wondering whether you would have code somewhere lying around for a beta version of function occu() which would allow for this ?

Thanks and best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Perhaps there is an advantage of coding up an alternate likelihood in terms of some saved statistical power to estimate other parameters, but if you wanted an easy life - would it not be simpler for your colleagues to account for unequal occasion lengths by fixing a simple site-by-occasion "duration" covariate on p?

I wouldn't even give this a second thought.... so I wonder what am I not seeing?

Josh

Ken

I will probably give it a try and will share with the group if I get to it.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: New unmarked version 1.5.0
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

A new version of unmarked (1.5.0) is now on CRAN. It may take some time before packages are available on all platforms.

Changes:

* Added community occupancy model (occuComm); i.e., occupancy model with species-level random effects [1]. See the vignette here: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/unmarked/vignettes/occuComm.html
* Support for hazard key function in IDS()
* Updates, improvements, standardization for many unmarkedFit methods such as getP, fitted, residuals, ranef, simulate, etc. IMPORTANT: these changes may break old code in some rare cases [2].
* Improved documentation for the functions above
* Bugfixes, including a fix to the goccu() likelihood discussed here: https://groups.google.com/g/unmarked/c/iH6yhkH_tFc

[1] Technically it was already possible to fit this model with the available random effects tools in occu(). The new function makes specifying the inputs and processing the model outputs easier.

[2] I try very hard to not break backwards compatability, but I feel it was necessary in this case. Historically methods for examining fitted models such as fitted(), residuals(), and ranef() have inconsistently handled missing values, particularly cases where all observations for a site were missing. By default, sometimes these sites were dropped and other times they were retained in the output. So if you had 100 sites and one had all missing values, some functions returned output of length 99 and others returned output of length 100. Going forward the output dimensions should always match the inputs - sites with all missing values will never be dropped. As part of these changes, 'na.rm' arguments for these methods will now be ignored. My strong opinion is that handling missing values in the output of these functions should be done by the user, not the package, to minimize the chances of unexpected behavior. Note that this changes nothing about how missing values are handled *when fitting the model* - this still works the same way. These changes apply only to functions liked residuals, ranef, etc. that are used on already fitted models.

Please let me know if you run into any issues with the new version.

Thanks,

Ken

Historically methods for examining fitted models such as fitted(), residuals(), and ranef() have inconsistently handled missing values, particularly cases where all observations for a site were missing. By default, sometimes these sites were dropped and other times they were retained in the output. So if you had 100 sites and one had all missing values, some functions returned output of length 99 and others returned output of length 100. Going forward the output dimensions should always match the inputs - sites with all missing values will never be dropped. As part of these changes, 'na.rm' arguments for these methods will now be ignored. My strong opinion is that handling missing values in the output of these functions should be done by the user, not the package, to minimize the chances of unexpected behavior. Note that this changes nothing about how missing values are handled *when fitting the model* - this still works the same way. These changes apply only to functions liked residuals, ranef, etc. that are used on already fitted models.

messages.subject: how to choose best occasion length and k-value in pcount
messages.subject_clean: how to choose best occasion length and k-value in pcount
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am working on a
N-Mix model to estimate deer abundance using a CT design in a study period of
ca. 3 winter months when there is no migration, to respect the assumption of
population closure. I know N-mix model is not highly reccomended for CT
studies but I read multiple articles where it is shown that it can still
provide reliable results.

I would like to ask
you a suggestion on how to decide for the correct occasion length in
combination with the correct K value.

My idea was to run
multiple global models (including all "biological-relevant" covariates) with different occasion length
(5, 7, 12, 15 days), and for each occasion length running multiple models with
different K-values. Once I see what is the best K-value for each occasion
length, I want to run a
Goodness of Fit test to see which occasion length provides the best fit. Once I
get the best fitting model I will be able to do some model selection to choose
which covariates to keep and which not, using the pre-selected occasion length and K-values.

 However, while this
approach seemed to me the most logical, it also implies running a lots of model
which will require very long computational time. Plus, I am not sure if it
makes complete sense to run this comparison on models with all the covariates
if then I will probably exclude some (likely changing the fitness of the model).
Also, if I run all these models with e.g. a Poisson distribution but then none
of them fits well the data, should I re-run everything with a different
distribution (e.g. NB or ZIP) and decide again for the best K-value and
occasion length?

I hope I explained
the problem cleared enough and any suggestions/critics on how to select these
two parameters are very welcome.

Thank you in
advance!

Walter

messages.subject: Optimal analysis small dataset
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I was wondering if anyone could give me some tips. I've been working with CT data in a wildlife-corridor for my master thesis, and my original plan was to perform a multi-species occupancy model using wolf-prey data (wild boar, red deer and roe deer). Unfortunately, I don't have a lot of sites (34), but I do have a long survey period (April-November). I've tried collapsing into 1 and 2 weeks, and only selecting summer months, but besides sampling effort and distance to closest trail, I don't have any detection covariates. Basically, my model is having trouble converging no matter how few covariates I use (shocker), unless I use the likelihood penalty, which changes my results so drastically that I'm a bit weary of using it. It shifts co-occurence to be very likely. My single-species models are not performing much better: especially for deer, since their occupancy is non significant and adding any site covariate gives a p of 1.

I was wondering if it makes sense to use occuRN for single-species models, to account for detection heterogeneity? Is this large survey effort an issue? Does anyone have any other tips I can try out?

Thanks a lot in advance!

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] how to choose best occasion length and k-value in pcount
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] how to choose best occasion length and k-value in pcount
messages.body_plain:
I think the choice of occasion length should depend more on what most reasonably meets the assumptions of the N-mixture model in your system, and less on what appears to fit best. The assumption of the N-mix model is that within an occasion, every count represents a set of unique individual animals. If you have 10 deer pictures over a 15 day period, how confident are you that these pictures represent 10 unique deer? What about 10 deer pictures over a 5 day period? It seems to me that the the longer the period, the more likely you are to be double-counting the same deer within an occasion. I think this probably likely even with an occasion length of only 1 day, unless you can uniquely identify deer in photos. So I guess I fall in the camp of believing N-mixture is not a great idea with camera data in most cases.

I would not worry so much about the K-value. Just pick one value you know to be bigger than the uppermost reasonable true abundance for these sites. The only cost to 'overestimating' K is slightly longer model fit times. If you find you are needing to change K as you change the occasion length, that is pretty good evidence that you are probably not meeting the assumptions of the model (because it implies that latent abundance is changing as a function of occasion length, which makes no sense if the model assumptions are met).

There are a few past discussions of abundance distribution choice (Poission/NB) on the listserv. You might also look at section 6.9.3 Kery & Royle volume 1. A common finding seems to be that NB will fit better but provide worse predictions. So making the choice based solely on goodness-of-fit might not be a good idea.

Ken

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Optimal analysis small dataset
messages.body_plain:
With only 34 sites, I definitely would not try anything more complicated than a 2-species model (it's not clear from your email if you tried several separate pairwise models with wolf or one single model with all 4 species). This model requires a lot of data to have adequate power and 34 sites is likely not enough even for a 2 species model, although it depends on detection probability, number of occasions, and covariates.

I think you are right to be wary of the penalized likelihood results - penalized likelihood can't fix a low sample size. However if the non-penalized model has very large parameter estimates and/or SEs (say >~5) then I wouldn't trust those results either.

My recommendations really depend on what your key objectives are. If looking at species interactions is not a crucial goal, I'd focus on single-species occupancy. It sounds like you're having trouble with those too (which if so, definitely don't go on to the more complicated multispecies model). I would think 34 sites should be enough for relatively simple single-species occuppancy models, though. Perhaps deer are just detected at every site and that's why you're getting strange results for that model? If so there's no reason to do an occupancy model - you already know they are everywhere.

You could try occuRN but just based on your email I don't see a specific reason why it would help.

Ken

messages.subject: Re: Optimal analysis small dataset
messages.body_plain:
One approach that might work depending on objective would be to focus on p effects vs psi effects. If there are many occasions, you might have more power than the 34 sites provide for psi interactions, as Ken mentions. For example, species A being present or being detected (at some point ever, or some recent point) might influence the detection probability of species B or vice versa. My very limited observation is that this sort of pattern tends to be more common than conditional occupancy effects when focusing on predator-prey interactions.

I honestly don't remember whether the Rota et al. models or their implementation here really touch on conditional detection probabilities. If not, the older "two-species" models of MacKenzie et al. (2006) or Richmond et al. (2010) did, and I think these are still options in MARK/PRESENCE/their R-wrappers?

John

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] how to choose best occasion length and k-value in pcount
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] how to choose best occasion length and k-value in pcount
messages.body_plain:
Dear Ken,

Thank you very much for your answer, your suggestions to go after the assumption rather than the fitness makes complete sense.

To minimize the risk of non-independent detection, I will try to reduce the occasion length (maybe staying between 3 and 7 days), keeping in mind that the possibility of false positives remains high. However, I believe an N-Mix model is still the best choice for my study, as it allows to account for imperfect detection. But more importantly, because my primary interest is in estimating the utilization density of a site rather than absolute abundance, as my goal is to use the model’s predictions to assess the impact of deer on browsing pressure. Whether the same deer visits a site multiple times or different individuals do, the overall impact on the vegetation remains the same,  as they all contribute to the browsing pressure (3 individuals going to a site once within an occasion will have the same impact of 1 individual going there three times within an occasion and thus non-independent detection should become a smaller problem). Additionally, we already have quite a good overview on deer distribution in my study area and so I will be able to check if the results of the model will meet the expectations or not.

Regarding the K-values,  I was worried about it mainly for the computational times and so I was looking for a way to find the smallest K that was still providing stable results. Maybe for that I will follow  Kery et al. (2018), who suggests to define K value as K=max(Ci,t) + 100.

Finally, thank you for the advise on the distribution, I did read the book you mentioned and, as I need to produce predictions, using a Poisson seems to be the better option (however, I still find it counterintuitive that a model that fits the data better produce worse predictions...).

Thank you again for your insights. I would be very interested in knowing your thoughts on my approach now that I explained better what I need the model for (hopefully this is one of the cases where using an N-Mix model for CT data is still justified!).

Best!

Walter

Il giorno mercoledì 12 febbraio 2025 alle 15:31:59 UTC+1 Ken Kellner ha scritto:
> I think the choice of occasion length should depend more on what most reasonably meets the assumptions of the N-mixture model in your system, and less on what appears to fit best. The assumption of the N-mix model is that within an occasion, every count represents a set of unique individual animals. If you have 10 deer pictures over a 15 day period, how confident are you that these pictures represent 10 unique deer? What about 10 deer pictures over a 5 day period? It seems to me that the the longer the period, the more likely you are to be double-counting the same deer within an occasion. I think this probably likely even with an occasion length of only 1 day, unless you can uniquely identify deer in photos. So I guess I fall in the camp of believing N-mixture is not a great idea with camera data in most cases.
>
> I would not worry so much about the K-value. Just pick one value you know to be bigger than the uppermost reasonable true abundance for these sites. The only cost to 'overestimating' K is slightly longer model fit times. If you find you are needing to change K as you change the occasion length, that is pretty good evidence that you are probably not meeting the assumptions of the model (because it implies that latent abundance is changing as a function of occasion length, which makes no sense if the model assumptions are met).
>
> There are a few past discussions of abundance distribution choice (Poission/NB) on the listserv. You might also look at section 6.9.3 Kery & Royle volume 1. A common finding seems to be that NB will fit better but provide worse predictions. So making the choice based solely on goodness-of-fit might not be a good idea.
>
> Ken
>
>
>
> On Wed, Feb 12, 2025 at 02:47:32AM -0800, Walter Di Nicola wrote:
> >
> >
> > Hello,
> >
> > I am working on a N-Mix model to estimate deer abundance using a CT design
> > in a study period of ca. 3 winter months when there is no migration, to
> > respect the assumption of population closure. I know N-mix model is not
> > highly reccomended for CT studies but I read multiple articles where it is
> > shown that it can still provide reliable results.
> >
> > I would like to ask you a suggestion on how to decide for the correct
> > occasion length in combination with the correct K value.
> >
> > My idea was to run multiple global models (including all
> > "biological-relevant" covariates) with different occasion length (5, 7, 12,
> > 15 days), and for each occasion length running multiple models with
> > different K-values. Once I see what is the best K-value for each occasion
> > length, I want to run a Goodness of Fit test to see which occasion length
> > provides the best fit. Once I get the best fitting model I will be able to
> > do some model selection to choose which covariates to keep and which not,
> > using the pre-selected occasion length and K-values.
> >
> > However, while this approach seemed to me the most logical, it also
> > implies running a lots of model which will require very long computational
> > time. Plus, I am not sure if it makes complete sense to run this comparison
> > on models with all the covariates if then I will probably exclude some

> > with e.g. a Poisson distribution but then none of them fits well the data,
> > should I re-run everything with a different distribution (e.g. NB or ZIP)
> > and decide again for the best K-value and occasion length?
> >
> > I hope I explained the problem cleared enough and any suggestions/critics

> >

> >

messages.subject: problem with occupancy model fitting
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a removal-design occupancy data set with 4400 sites, 3 occasions and the species of interest (long-eared owl) observed at 256 sites, yielding a detection-naive occupancy of  6%. When trying to fit even the simplest occupancy model with two intercepts, I get a numerical failure:

Occupancy (logit-scale):
 Estimate  SE   z P(>|z|)
     3.58 NaN NaN     NaN

Detection (logit-scale):
 Estimate  SE   z P(>|z|)
    -3.87 NaN NaN     NaN

...
Warnmeldungen:
1: In sqrt(diag(vcov(obj, fixedOnly = fixedOnly))) : NaNs wurden erzeugt
2: In sqrt(diag(vcov(obj, fixedOnly = fixedOnly))) : NaNs wurden erzeugt

I tried to make unmarked/optim's job a little easier by providing initial values 'c(qlogis(256/3498), 0)' and setting 'method = "BFGS"', but that didn't help either:

Occupancy (logit-scale):
 Estimate  SE   z P(>|z|)
     1.31 NaN NaN     NaN

Detection (logit-scale):
 Estimate  SE   z P(>|z|)
    -3.65 NaN NaN     NaN

1: In sqrt(diag(vcov(obj, fixedOnly = fixedOnly))) : NaNs wurden erzeugt
2: In sqrt(diag(vcov(obj, fixedOnly = fixedOnly))) : NaNs wurden erzeugt

Anybody has any ideas, other than trying out many different sets of inits (or going Bayesian) ?

Thanks and best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
hi Marc,
 It's possible in this case that the likelihood does not have a maximum or rather the likelihood is increasing as p -> 0, psi->1. So this kind of boundary situation produces unstable looking MLEs and invalid frequentist inferences. It would be interesting to look at a bi-plot of (logit(p), logit(psi)) in the corner of the parameter space around [p=0, psi = 1].
regards
andy

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] problem with occupancy model fitting
messages.body_plain:
For diagnosing issues with the simple/basic model, I use psi and p rather than the logits of those parameters.  I generated data from the simple model to get similar histories as yours with psi=0.1 and p=0.025 and a maximum of 3 visits and 4400 sites.  The history frequencies are

> History   Frequency
> 000       4144
> 1          120
> 01          83
> 001         53

So a total of 120+83+53 = 256 detections.  The contour plot of the log likelihood with the starting values and the resulting maximum likelihood estimates looks like the following:

The above was done by writing code in Mathematica where one can control the precision of the calculations (as double precision isn't always enough - which is what I believe all of the unmarked functions use).  Because nothing looks out of the ordinary so maybe it's a need for better starting values.  Here's R code that gets results that match the likelihood surface above.

> library(unmarked)

> M <- 4400
> J <- 3

> y <- matrix(c(rep(0,4144*3), rep(c(0, 0, 1), 53), rep(c(0, 1, NA), 83),
>      rep(c(1, NA, NA), 120)), M, J, byrow=TRUE)

> umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y)

> fit <- occu(~1~1, umf, starts=c(log(0.083/(1-0.083)), log(0.332/(1-0.332))))
> fit
>
resulting in the following:

> Call:
> occu(formula = ~1 ~ 1, data = umf, starts = c(log(0.083/(1 - 0.083)), log(0.332/(1 - 0.332))))

> Occupancy:

>  Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)

>      -2.4 0.129 -18.6 2.18e-77

> Detection:

>  Estimate   SE     z P(>|z|)

>      -0.7 0.24 -2.92 0.00355

It seems to be the situation that good starting values are your best friends.

Jim

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] problem with occupancy model fitting
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jim, all,

this is fantastic, thank you very much. Of course, if one can do things analytically, then this is superior to a brute force solution by simulation. (But the thing is of course that most people, including myself, can't do that and so....).

Anyway, good to know that theoretically the long-eared owl removal occupancy model should be estimable under the conditions studied. BTW, my actual detection history frequencies are:
4142 times '000'
148 times '001'
22 times '01'
86 times '1'

Now, importantly, my first model was mis-specified in the sense of assuming equal occasion length. However, occasions are very uneven in length, being 2, 0.75 and 5.25 mins. So I next accounted for this in the model (in JAGS, where I find this trivially easy to code up) as follows. Fitting this second model gave very different estimates from the first, mis-specified one and had much better traceplots.

  for (i in 1:nSites) {
    # True state model for the partially observed true state
    z[i] ~ dbern(psi)

    # Observation model for the actual observations scaled to 1 min units
    y[i,1] ~ dbern(z[i] * (1 - (1-p)^2))      # First occasion
    y[i,2] ~ dbern(z[i] * (1 - (1-p)^0.75))   # Second occasion
    y[i,3] ~ dbern(z[i] * (1 - (1-p)^5.25))   # Third occasion
  }

Here is the traceplot and posterior summary for the mis-specified first model (4 chains with 500k length, 250k burnin, and thinning by 1/250):
               mean      sd     2.5%      50%    97.5% overlap0 f  Rhat n.eff
psi         0.729   0.178    0.350    0.751    0.988    FALSE 1 1.006   403
p           0.030   0.010    0.019    0.027    0.058    FALSE 1 1.009   445

And here is the traceplot and posterior summary for the second model with proper scaling of detection probability to 1 min units (4 chains with 100k length, 10k burnin, and thinning by 1/90):
                         mean      sd    2.5%      50%    97.5% overlap0 f  Rhat n.eff
psi         0.170   0.141   0.082    0.125    0.700    FALSE 1 1.081   138
p           0.075   0.033   0.011    0.076    0.137    FALSE 1 1.006   618

Although the second analysis is not fantastic in terms of mixing, I consider it far better than the first (why ? well, for once because there can't be 0.729 * 4400 = 3200 long-eared owls in the study area .... while 748 is in the realm of the possible).

I intend to "penalize" psi now some, e.g., by use of a beta(1, 5) prior and will see where this gets me. The main interest of my colleagues is in patterns of detection probability, e.g., related to playback vs. no playback, survey date and incidence of a tawny owl hooting or not.

Best regards  --- Marc

Hi Walter,

I think this seems reasonable, particularly if you are mainly interested in an index of relative abundance.

You could also just use the intensity of detections as the index, I suppose, as a simpler option. You couldn't estimate a separate detection probability but that might not matter depending on how you expect p to vary over space/time.

Ken

On Thu, Feb 13, 2025 at 04:33:31AM -0800, Walter Di Nicola wrote:
> Dear Ken,
>
> Thank you very much for your answer, your suggestions to go after the
> assumption rather than the fitness makes complete sense.
>
> To minimize the risk of non-independent detection, I will try to reduce the
> occasion length (maybe staying between 3 and 7 days), keeping in mind that
> the possibility of false positives remains high. However, I believe an
> N-Mix model is still the best choice for my study, as it allows to account
> for imperfect detection. But more importantly, because my primary interest

> is in estimating the *utilization density* of a site rather than absolute

> abundance, as my goal is to use the model’s predictions to assess the
> impact of deer on browsing pressure. Whether the same deer visits a site
> multiple times or different individuals do, the overall impact on the
> vegetation remains the same,  as they all contribute to the browsing
> pressure (3 individuals going to a site once within an occasion will have
> the same impact of 1 individual going there three times within an occasion
> and thus non-independent detection should become a smaller problem).
> Additionally, we already have quite a good overview on deer distribution in
> my study area and so I will be able to check if the results of the model
> will meet the expectations or not.
>
> Regarding the K-values,  I was worried about it mainly for the
> computational times and so I was looking for a way to find the smallest K
> that was still providing stable results. Maybe for that I will follow  Kery
> et al. (2018), who suggests to define K value as K=max(Ci,t) + 100.
>
> Finally, thank you for the advise on the distribution, I did read the book
> you mentioned and, as I need to produce predictions, using a Poisson seems
> to be the better option (however, I still find it counterintuitive that a
> model that fits the data better produce worse predictions...).
>
> Thank you again for your insights. I would be very interested in knowing
> your thoughts on my approach now that I explained better what I need the
> model for (hopefully this is one of the cases where using an N-Mix model
> for CT data is still justified!).
>
> Best!
>
> Walter
>
>
> Il giorno mercoledì 12 febbraio 2025 alle 15:31:59 UTC+1 Ken Kellner ha
> scritto:
>
> > I think the choice of occasion length should depend more on what most
> > reasonably meets the assumptions of the N-mixture model in your system, and
> > less on what appears to fit best. The assumption of the N-mix model is that
> > within an occasion, every count represents a set of unique individual
> > animals. If you have 10 deer pictures over a 15 day period, how confident
> > are you that these pictures represent 10 unique deer? What about 10 deer
> > pictures over a 5 day period? It seems to me that the the longer the
> > period, the more likely you are to be double-counting the same deer within
> > an occasion. I think this probably likely even with an occasion length of
> > only 1 day, unless you can uniquely identify deer in photos. So I guess I
> > fall in the camp of believing N-mixture is not a great idea with camera
> > data in most cases.
> >
> > I would not worry so much about the K-value. Just pick one value you know
> > to be bigger than the uppermost reasonable true abundance for these sites.
> > The only cost to 'overestimating' K is slightly longer model fit times. If
> > you find you are needing to change K as you change the occasion length,
> > that is pretty good evidence that you are probably not meeting the
> > assumptions of the model (because it implies that latent abundance is
> > changing as a function of occasion length, which makes no sense if the
> > model assumptions are met).
> >
> > There are a few past discussions of abundance distribution choice
> > (Poission/NB) on the listserv. You might also look at section 6.9.3 Kery &
> > Royle volume 1. A common finding seems to be that NB will fit better but
> > provide worse predictions. So making the choice based solely on
> > goodness-of-fit might not be a good idea.
> >
> > Ken
> >
> >
> >
> > On Wed, Feb 12, 2025 at 02:47:32AM -0800, Walter Di Nicola wrote:
> > >
> > >
> > > Hello,
> > >
> > > I am working on a N-Mix model to estimate deer abundance using a CT
> > design
> > > in a study period of ca. 3 winter months when there is no migration, to
> > > respect the assumption of population closure. I know N-mix model is not
> > > highly reccomended for CT studies but I read multiple articles where it
> > is
> > > shown that it can still provide reliable results.
> > >
> > > I would like to ask you a suggestion on how to decide for the correct
> > > occasion length in combination with the correct K value.
> > >
> > > My idea was to run multiple global models (including all
> > > "biological-relevant" covariates) with different occasion length (5, 7,
> > 12,
> > > 15 days), and for each occasion length running multiple models with
> > > different K-values. Once I see what is the best K-value for each
> > occasion
> > > length, I want to run a Goodness of Fit test to see which occasion
> > length
> > > provides the best fit. Once I get the best fitting model I will be able
> > to
> > > do some model selection to choose which covariates to keep and which
> > not,
> > > using the pre-selected occasion length and K-values.
> > >
> > > However, while this approach seemed to me the most logical, it also
> > > implies running a lots of model which will require very long

> > > time. Plus, I am not sure if it makes complete sense to run this
> > comparison
> > > on models with all the covariates if then I will probably exclude some

> > models
> > > with e.g. a Poisson distribution but then none of them fits well the

> > > should I re-run everything with a different distribution (e.g. NB or
> > ZIP)
> > > and decide again for the best K-value and occasion length?
> > >
> > > I hope I explained the problem cleared enough and any

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the specific history counts.  Here is the resulting contour plot of the log likelihood:

We see that the maximum likelihood estimate of psi is 1.0  So occu was doing things correctly.  Why  the estimate of 1 for psi?  The 3 possible histories at sites with at least one detection are 001, 01, and 1 for the removal design with a maximum of 3 visits.  The associated probabilities are (1-p)^2 * p, (1-p) * p, and p, respectively.  We see that
(1-p)^2 * p < (1-p) * p < p and most of the time we expect the associated counts (n001, n01, and n1) to have that same ordering.

For your example n001 = 148, n01 = 22, and n1 = 86.  We see that n1 is much less than n001 which is not expected when visits are independent and have the same detection probability.  This also results in the maximum likelihood estimate of psi being 1.0.

I speculate that anytime n1 is less than or equal to n001, the maximum likelihood estimate for psi will be 1.  Further the estimate of psi will also be 1 whenever n1 isn't much larger than n001.  (I'm going to look into this further to see if there is more specific and justifiable inferences about this.)

All of this suggests that maybe the independence assumption is false or that the probabilities vary by the visit number (or some other deviation from the usual assumptions).

If one considers different probabilities for each visit, then occu will give estimates and a much, much lower AIC value. I clearly don't know if that's a reasonable model for this species (and whoever does the surveying).

Jim

> Dear Jim, all,
>
> this is fantastic, thank you very much. Of course, if one can do things analytically, then this is superior to a brute force solution by simulation. (But the thing is of course that most people, including myself, can't do that and so....).
>
> Anyway, good to know that theoretically the long-eared owl removal occupancy model should be estimable under the conditions studied. BTW, my actual detection history frequencies are:
> 4142 times '000'
> 148 times '001'
> 22 times '01'
> 86 times '1'
>
>
> Now, importantly, my first model was mis-specified in the sense of assuming equal occasion length. However, occasions are very uneven in length, being 2, 0.75 and 5.25 mins. So I next accounted for this in the model (in JAGS, where I find this trivially easy to code up) as follows. Fitting this second model gave very different estimates from the first, mis-specified one and had much better traceplots.
>
>   for (i in 1:nSites) {
>     # True state model for the partially observed true state
>     z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
>
>     # Observation model for the actual observations scaled to 1 min units
>     y[i,1] ~ dbern(z[i] * (1 - (1-p)^2))      # First occasion
>     y[i,2] ~ dbern(z[i] * (1 - (1-p)^0.75))   # Second occasion
>     y[i,3] ~ dbern(z[i] * (1 - (1-p)^5.25))   # Third occasion
>   }
>
> Here is the traceplot and posterior summary for the mis-specified first model (4 chains with 500k length, 250k burnin, and thinning by 1/250):
>                mean      sd     2.5%      50%    97.5% overlap0 f  Rhat n.eff
> psi         0.729   0.178    0.350    0.751    0.988    FALSE 1 1.006   403
> p           0.030   0.010    0.019    0.027    0.058    FALSE 1 1.009   445
>
>
> And here is the traceplot and posterior summary for the second model with proper scaling of detection probability to 1 min units (4 chains with 100k length, 10k burnin, and thinning by 1/90):
>                          mean      sd    2.5%      50%    97.5% overlap0 f  Rhat n.eff
> psi         0.170   0.141   0.082    0.125    0.700    FALSE 1 1.081   138
> p           0.075   0.033   0.011    0.076    0.137    FALSE 1 1.006   618
>

> Although the second analysis is not fantastic in terms of mixing, I consider it far better than the first (why ? well, for once because there can't be 0.729 * 4400 = 3200 long-eared owls in the study area .... while 748 is in the realm of the possible).
>
> I intend to "penalize" psi now some, e.g., by use of a beta(1, 5) prior and will see where this gets me. The main interest of my colleagues is in patterns of detection probability, e.g., related to playback vs. no playback, survey date and incidence of a tawny owl hooting or not.

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] problem with occupancy model fitting
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jim,

thank you very much. But if I understand this right, then your analysis does not incorporate unequal occasion length (2, 0.75, 5.25 min). I think that accounting for this should yield something not on the boundary of paramater space, since JAGS can't get it completely wrong (see 2nd set of trace plots below and table of estimates).

Best regards  --- Marc

From: unma...@googlegroups.com <unma...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Jim Baldwin <jbald...@gmail.com>

Sent: Saturday, February 15, 2025 01:33

To: unma...@googlegroups.com <unma...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: [unmarked] problem with occupancy model fitting

Thanks for the specific history counts.  Here is the resulting contour plot of the log likelihood:

We see that the maximum likelihood estimate of psi is 1.0  So occu was doing things correctly.  Why  the estimate of 1 for psi?  The 3 possible histories at sites with at least one detection are 001, 01, and 1 for the removal design with a maximum of 3 visits.  The associated probabilities are (1-p)^2 * p, (1-p) * p, and p, respectively.  We see that
(1-p)^2 * p < (1-p) * p < p and most of the time we expect the associated counts (n001, n01, and n1) to have that same ordering.

For your example n001 = 148, n01 = 22, and n1 = 86.  We see that n1 is much less than n001 which is not expected when visits are independent and have the same detection probability.  This also results in the maximum likelihood estimate of psi being 1.0.

I speculate that anytime n1 is less than or equal to n001, the maximum likelihood estimate for psi will be 1.  Further the estimate of psi will also be 1 whenever n1 isn't much larger than n001.  (I'm going to look into this further to see if there is more specific and justifiable inferences about this.)

All of this suggests that maybe the independence assumption is false or that the probabilities vary by the visit number (or some other deviation from the usual assumptions).

If one considers different probabilities for each visit, then occu will give estimates and a much, much lower AIC value. I clearly don't know if that's a reasonable model for this species (and whoever does the surveying).

Jim

On Fri, Feb 14, 2025 at 1:37 AM Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch> wrote:
> Dear Jim, all,
>
> this is fantastic, thank you very much. Of course, if one can do things analytically, then this is superior to a brute force solution by simulation. (But the thing is of course that most people, including myself, can't do that and so....).
>
> Anyway, good to know that theoretically the long-eared owl removal occupancy model should be estimable under the conditions studied. BTW, my actual detection history frequencies are:
> 4142 times '000'
> 148 times '001'
> 22 times '01'
> 86 times '1'
>
>
> Now, importantly, my first model was mis-specified in the sense of assuming equal occasion length. However, occasions are very uneven in length, being 2, 0.75 and 5.25 mins. So I next accounted for this in the model (in JAGS, where I find this trivially easy to code up) as follows. Fitting this second model gave very different estimates from the first, mis-specified one and had much better traceplots.
>
>   for (i in 1:nSites) {
>     # True state model for the partially observed true state
>     z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
>
>     # Observation model for the actual observations scaled to 1 min units
>     y[i,1] ~ dbern(z[i] * (1 - (1-p)^2))      # First occasion
>     y[i,2] ~ dbern(z[i] * (1 - (1-p)^0.75))   # Second occasion
>     y[i,3] ~ dbern(z[i] * (1 - (1-p)^5.25))   # Third occasion
>   }
>
> Here is the traceplot and posterior summary for the mis-specified first model (4 chains with 500k length, 250k burnin, and thinning by 1/250):
>                mean      sd     2.5%      50%    97.5% overlap0 f  Rhat n.eff
> psi         0.729   0.178    0.350    0.751    0.988    FALSE 1 1.006   403
> p           0.030   0.010    0.019    0.027    0.058    FALSE 1 1.009   445
>
>
> And here is the traceplot and posterior summary for the second model with proper scaling of detection probability to 1 min units (4 chains with 100k length, 10k burnin, and thinning by 1/90):
>                          mean      sd    2.5%      50%    97.5% overlap0 f  Rhat n.eff
> psi         0.170   0.141   0.082    0.125    0.700    FALSE 1 1.081   138
> p           0.075   0.033   0.011    0.076    0.137    FALSE 1 1.006   618
>
>
> Although the second analysis is not fantastic in terms of mixing, I consider it far better than the first (why ? well, for once because there can't be 0.729 * 4400 = 3200 long-eared owls in the study area .... while 748 is in the realm of the possible).
>
> I intend to "penalize" psi now some, e.g., by use of a beta(1, 5) prior and will see where this gets me. The main interest of my colleagues is in patterns of detection probability, e.g., related to playback vs. no playback, survey date and incidence of a tawny owl hooting or not.
>
> Best regards  --- Marc
>
>
>
