messages.subject: Performing validation for PCount model with detection process
messages.subject_clean: Performing validation for PCount model with detection process
messages.body_plain:
I am using an unmarked PCount model to predicted abundance and detection of a presence-only dataset. Give that the detection process helps to adjust the predicted abundance based on where detection is more or less likely, I am wondering what the best way to perform model validation would be? I have tried several models with slightly different combinations of covariates and want to select the one that is most representative.
Given that the training dataset is low sample size and skewed by the detection factors, does anyone know of best practices / methods of performing model validation for pcount models? Please also share any good examples in the literature if you know of any.
Thank you!

messages.body_plain:
My feeble excuse is that once I saw the frequency counts for the histories, I rushed to put together the contour plot and didn't yet read down further for the new information.

So taking into account the occasion length the log likelihood contour plot looks like the following:

Following the suggestion by Andy, a more close-up view in the lower, left-hand corner is the following:

Here is some general R code that finds the maximum likelihood estimates of psi and p for a removal design with a maximum of 3 visits and different occasion lengths:

logL <- function(parms, n000, n001, n01, n1, e1, e2, e3) {
  # Log of the likelihood function
  # n000, n001, n01, and n1 are the history counts
  # e1, e2, and e3 are the occasion lengths
  p <- parms[1]
  psi <- parms[2]
  n1*(log(1 - (1 - p)^e1) + log(psi)) +
  n01*(log(1 - (1 - p)^e2) + log((1 - p)^e1) + log(psi)) +
  n001*(log(1 - (1 - p)^e3) + log((1 - p)^e2) + log((1 - p)^e1) + log(psi)) +
  n000*log(1 - psi + psi*(1 - p)^(e1+e2+e3))
}

fit <- optim(c(0.5, 0.5), logL, n000=4142, n001=148, n01=22, n1=86,
  e1=2, e2=0.75, e3=5.25, lower=c(1,1)/10000, upper=c(1,1)-1/10000,
  method="L-BFGS-B", control=list(fnscale=-1), hessian=TRUE)

se <- diag(-solve(fit$hessian))
cat("Parameter\tEstimate\tStd. Err.\n",
    "psi      \t", fit$par[2], "\t", se[2], "\n",
    "p        \t", fit$par[1], "\t", se[1], "\n",
    "AIC      \t", -2*fit$value+2*2, "\n", sep="")

# Parameter       Estimate        Std. Err.
# psi             0.1119926       0.0007510308
# p               0.08760724      0.0008565208
# AIC             2415.84

Jim

> Dear Jim,

I think that accounting for this should yield something not on the boundary of paramater space, since JAGS can't get it completely wrong (see 2nd set of trace plots below and table of estimates).

> Subject: Re: [unmarked] problem with occupancy model fitting
>
> Thanks for the specific history counts.  Here is the resulting contour plot of the log likelihood:
>
> We see that the maximum likelihood estimate of psi is 1.0  So occu was doing things correctly.  Why  the estimate of 1 for psi?  The 3 possible histories at sites with at least one detection are 001, 01, and 1 for the removal design with a maximum of 3 visits.  The associated probabilities are (1-p)^2 * p, (1-p) * p, and p, respectively.  We see that
> (1-p)^2 * p < (1-p) * p < p and most of the time we expect the associated counts (n001, n01, and n1) to have that same ordering.
>
> For your example n001 = 148, n01 = 22, and n1 = 86.  We see that n1 is much less than n001 which is not expected when visits are independent and have the same detection probability.  This also results in the maximum likelihood estimate of psi being 1.0.
>
> I speculate that anytime n1 is less than or equal to n001, the maximum likelihood estimate for psi will be 1.  Further the estimate of psi will also be 1 whenever n1 isn't much larger than n001.  (I'm going to look into this further to see if there is more specific and justifiable inferences about this.)
>
> All of this suggests that maybe the independence assumption is false or that the probabilities vary by the visit number (or some other deviation from the usual assumptions).
>
> If one considers different probabilities for each visit, then occu will give estimates and a much, much lower AIC value. I clearly don't know if that's a reasonable model for this species (and whoever does the surveying).
>
> Jim
>
>
>

> On Fri, Feb 14, 2025 at 1:37 AM Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch> wrote:

> > 4142 times '000'

> > Now, importantly, my first model was mis-specified in the sense of assuming equal occasion length. However, occasions are very uneven in length, being 2, 0.75 and 5.25 mins. So I next accounted for this in the model (in JAGS, where I find this trivially easy to code up) as follows. Fitting this second model gave very different estimates from the first, mis-specified one and had much better traceplots.

> >     y[i,2] ~ dbern(z[i] * (1 - (1-p)^0.75))   # Second occasion
> >     y[i,3] ~ dbern(z[i] * (1 - (1-p)^5.25))   # Third occasion
> >   }

> > Here is the traceplot and posterior summary for the mis-specified first model (4 chains with 500k length, 250k burnin, and thinning by 1/250):

> >
> >
> > And here is the traceplot and posterior summary for the second model with proper scaling of detection probability to 1 min units (4 chains with 100k length, 10k burnin, and thinning by 1/90):
> >                          mean      sd    2.5%      50%    97.5% overlap0 f  Rhat n.eff

> >

> >
> > I intend to "penalize" psi now some, e.g., by use of a beta(1, 5) prior and will see where this gets me. The main interest of my colleagues is in patterns of detection probability, e.g., related to playback vs. no playback, survey date and incidence of a tawny owl hooting or not.

messages.body_plain:
Crap.  I'm getting t0o sloppy in my old age.  I forgot to take the square root of the variances to get the standard errors.  Here's a correction.

logL <- function(parms, n000, n001, n01, n1, e1, e2, e3) {
  # Log of the likelihood function
  # n000, n001, n01, and n1 are the history counts
  # e1, e2, and e3 are the occasion lengths
  p <- parms[1]
  psi <- parms[2]
  n1*(log(1 - (1 - p)^e1) + log(psi)) +
  n01*(log(1 - (1 - p)^e2) + log((1 - p)^e1) + log(psi)) +
  n001*(log(1 - (1 - p)^e3) + log((1 - p)^e2) + log((1 - p)^e1) + log(psi)) +
  n000*log(1 - psi + psi*(1 - p)^(e1+e2+e3))
}

fit <- optim(c(0.5, 0.5), logL, n000=4142, n001=148, n01=22, n1=86,
  e1=2, e2=0.75, e3=5.25, lower=c(1,1)/10000, upper=c(1,1)-1/10000,
  method="L-BFGS-B", control=list(fnscale=-1), hessian=TRUE)

se <- diag(-solve(fit$hessian))^0.5

cat("Parameter\tEstimate\tStd. Err.\n",
    "psi      \t", fit$par[2], "\t", se[2], "\n",
    "p        \t", fit$par[1], "\t", se[1], "\n",
    "AIC      \t", -2*fit$value+2*2, "\n", sep="")

# Parameter       Estimate        Std. Err.

# psi             0.1119926       0.02740494
# p               0.08760724      0.02926638
# AIC             2415.84

Jim

I think that accounting for this should yield something not on the boundary of paramater space, since JAGS can't get it completely wrong (see 2nd set of trace plots below and table of estimates).

> >
> > Thanks for the specific history counts.  Here is the resulting contour plot of the log likelihood:
> >
> > We see that the maximum likelihood estimate of psi is 1.0  So occu was doing things correctly.  Why  the estimate of 1 for psi?  The 3 possible histories at sites with at least one detection are 001, 01, and 1 for the removal design with a maximum of 3 visits.  The associated probabilities are (1-p)^2 * p, (1-p) * p, and p, respectively.  We see that
> > (1-p)^2 * p < (1-p) * p < p and most of the time we expect the associated counts (n001, n01, and n1) to have that same ordering.
> >
> > For your example n001 = 148, n01 = 22, and n1 = 86.  We see that n1 is much less than n001 which is not expected when visits are independent and have the same detection probability.  This also results in the maximum likelihood estimate of psi being 1.0.
> >
> > I speculate that anytime n1 is less than or equal to n001, the maximum likelihood estimate for psi will be 1.  Further the estimate of psi will also be 1 whenever n1 isn't much larger than n001.  (I'm going to look into this further to see if there is more specific and justifiable inferences about this.)
> >
> > All of this suggests that maybe the independence assumption is false or that the probabilities vary by the visit number (or some other deviation from the usual assumptions).
> >
> > If one considers different probabilities for each visit, then occu will give estimates and a much, much lower AIC value. I clearly don't know if that's a reasonable model for this species (and whoever does the surveying).
> >
> > Jim

So I next accounted for this in the model (in JAGS, where I find this trivially easy to code up) as follows. Fitting this second model gave very different estimates from the first, mis-specified one and had much better traceplots.

Il giorno venerdì 14 febbraio 2025 alle 14:12:37 UTC+1 Ken Kellner ha scritto:
> Hi Walter,
>
> I think this seems reasonable, particularly if you are mainly interested in an index of relative abundance.
>
> You could also just use the intensity of detections as the index, I suppose, as a simpler option. You couldn't estimate a separate detection probability but that might not matter depending on how you expect p to vary over space/time.
>
> Ken
>
> On Thu, Feb 13, 2025 at 04:33:31AM -0800, Walter Di Nicola wrote:
> > Dear Ken,
> >
> > Thank you very much for your answer, your suggestions to go after the
> > assumption rather than the fitness makes complete sense.
> >
> > To minimize the risk of non-independent detection, I will try to reduce the
> > occasion length (maybe staying between 3 and 7 days), keeping in mind that
> > the possibility of false positives remains high. However, I believe an
> > N-Mix model is still the best choice for my study, as it allows to account
> > for imperfect detection. But more importantly, because my primary interest
> > is in estimating the *utilization density* of a site rather than absolute
> > abundance, as my goal is to use the model’s predictions to assess the
> > impact of deer on browsing pressure. Whether the same deer visits a site
> > multiple times or different individuals do, the overall impact on the
> > vegetation remains the same, as they all contribute to the browsing
> > pressure (3 individuals going to a site once within an occasion will have
> > the same impact of 1 individual going there three times within an occasion
> > and thus non-independent detection should become a smaller problem).
> > Additionally, we already have quite a good overview on deer distribution in
> > my study area and so I will be able to check if the results of the model
> > will meet the expectations or not.
> >
> > Regarding the K-values, I was worried about it mainly for the
> > computational times and so I was looking for a way to find the smallest K
> > that was still providing stable results. Maybe for that I will follow Kery
> > et al. (2018), who suggests to define K value as K=max(Ci,t) + 100.
> >
> > Finally, thank you for the advise on the distribution, I did read the book
> > you mentioned and, as I need to produce predictions, using a Poisson seems
> > to be the better option (however, I still find it counterintuitive that a
> > model that fits the data better produce worse predictions...).
> >
> > Thank you again for your insights. I would be very interested in knowing
> > your thoughts on my approach now that I explained better what I need the
> > model for (hopefully this is one of the cases where using an N-Mix model
> > for CT data is still justified!).
> >
> > Best!
> >
> > Walter
> >
> >
> > Il giorno mercoledì 12 febbraio 2025 alle 15:31:59 UTC+1 Ken Kellner ha
> > scritto:
> >
> > > I think the choice of occasion length should depend more on what most
> > > reasonably meets the assumptions of the N-mixture model in your system, and
> > > less on what appears to fit best. The assumption of the N-mix model is that
> > > within an occasion, every count represents a set of unique individual
> > > animals. If you have 10 deer pictures over a 15 day period, how confident
> > > are you that these pictures represent 10 unique deer? What about 10 deer
> > > pictures over a 5 day period? It seems to me that the the longer the
> > > period, the more likely you are to be double-counting the same deer within
> > > an occasion. I think this probably likely even with an occasion length of
> > > only 1 day, unless you can uniquely identify deer in photos. So I guess I
> > > fall in the camp of believing N-mixture is not a great idea with camera
> > > data in most cases.
> > >
> > > I would not worry so much about the K-value. Just pick one value you know
> > > to be bigger than the uppermost reasonable true abundance for these sites.
> > > The only cost to 'overestimating' K is slightly longer model fit times. If
> > > you find you are needing to change K as you change the occasion length,
> > > that is pretty good evidence that you are probably not meeting the
> > > assumptions of the model (because it implies that latent abundance is
> > > changing as a function of occasion length, which makes no sense if the
> > > model assumptions are met).
> > >
> > > There are a few past discussions of abundance distribution choice
> > > (Poission/NB) on the listserv. You might also look at section 6.9.3 Kery &
> > > Royle volume 1. A common finding seems to be that NB will fit better but
> > > provide worse predictions. So making the choice based solely on
> > > goodness-of-fit might not be a good idea.
> > >
> > > Ken
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Wed, Feb 12, 2025 at 02:47:32AM -0800, Walter Di Nicola wrote:
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Hello,
> > > >
> > > > I am working on a N-Mix model to estimate deer abundance using a CT
> > > design
> > > > in a study period of ca. 3 winter months when there is no migration, to
> > > > respect the assumption of population closure. I know N-mix model is not
> > > > highly reccomended for CT studies but I read multiple articles where it
> > > is
> > > > shown that it can still provide reliable results.
> > > >
> > > > I would like to ask you a suggestion on how to decide for the correct
> > > > occasion length in combination with the correct K value.
> > > >
> > > > My idea was to run multiple global models (including all
> > > > "biological-relevant" covariates) with different occasion length (5, 7,
> > > 12,
> > > > 15 days), and for each occasion length running multiple models with
> > > > different K-values. Once I see what is the best K-value for each
> > > occasion
> > > > length, I want to run a Goodness of Fit test to see which occasion
> > > length
> > > > provides the best fit. Once I get the best fitting model I will be able
> > > to
> > > > do some model selection to choose which covariates to keep and which
> > > not,
> > > > using the pre-selected occasion length and K-values.
> > > >
> > > > However, while this approach seemed to me the most logical, it also
> > > > implies running a lots of model which will require very long
> > > computational
> > > > time. Plus, I am not sure if it makes complete sense to run this
> > > comparison
> > > > on models with all the covariates if then I will probably exclude some

> > > > should I re-run everything with a different distribution (e.g. NB or

> > > > I hope I explained the problem cleared enough and any
> > > suggestions/critics
> > > > on how to select these two parameters are very welcome.
> > > >
> > > > Thank you in advance!

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] problem with occupancy model fitting
messages.body_plain:
Superb, thank you very much, Jim !

Even though now I am doing a Bayesian analysis, it's of course based on the same likelihood and hence your analytical investigation provides some confidence that our data do let us estimate what we want.

Warm regards  --- Marc

From: unma...@googlegroups.com <unma...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Jim Baldwin <jbald...@gmail.com>

Sent: Saturday, February 15, 2025 20:22

To: unma...@googlegroups.com <unma...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: [unmarked] problem with occupancy model fitting

My feeble excuse is that once I saw the frequency counts for the histories, I rushed to put together the contour plot and didn't yet read down further for the new information.

So taking into account the occasion length the log likelihood contour plot looks like the following:

Following the suggestion by Andy, a more close-up view in the lower, left-hand corner is the following:

Here is some general R code that finds the maximum likelihood estimates of psi and p for a removal design with a maximum of 3 visits and different occasion lengths:

logL <- function(parms, n000, n001, n01, n1, e1, e2, e3) {
  # Log of the likelihood function
  # n000, n001, n01, and n1 are the history counts
  # e1, e2, and e3 are the occasion lengths
  p <- parms[1]
  psi <- parms[2]
  n1*(log(1 - (1 - p)^e1) + log(psi)) +
  n01*(log(1 - (1 - p)^e2) + log((1 - p)^e1) + log(psi)) +
  n001*(log(1 - (1 - p)^e3) + log((1 - p)^e2) + log((1 - p)^e1) + log(psi)) +
  n000*log(1 - psi + psi*(1 - p)^(e1+e2+e3))
}

fit <- optim(c(0.5, 0.5), logL, n000=4142, n001=148, n01=22, n1=86,
  e1=2, e2=0.75, e3=5.25, lower=c(1,1)/10000, upper=c(1,1)-1/10000,
  method="L-BFGS-B", control=list(fnscale=-1), hessian=TRUE)

se <- diag(-solve(fit$hessian))
cat("Parameter\tEstimate\tStd. Err.\n",
    "psi      \t", fit$par[2], "\t", se[2], "\n",
    "p        \t", fit$par[1], "\t", se[1], "\n",
    "AIC      \t", -2*fit$value+2*2, "\n", sep="")

# Parameter       Estimate        Std. Err.
# psi             0.1119926       0.0007510308
# p               0.08760724      0.0008565208
# AIC             2415.84

Jim

I think that accounting for this should yield something not on the boundary of paramater space, since JAGS can't get it completely wrong (see 2nd set of trace plots below and table of estimates).

> From: unma...@googlegroups.com <unma...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Jim Baldwin <jbald...@gmail.com>

>
> Thanks for the specific history counts.  Here is the resulting contour plot of the log likelihood:
>
> We see that the maximum likelihood estimate of psi is 1.0  So occu was doing things correctly.  Why  the estimate of 1 for psi?  The 3 possible histories at sites with at least one detection are 001, 01, and 1 for the removal design with a maximum of 3 visits.  The associated probabilities are (1-p)^2 * p, (1-p) * p, and p, respectively.  We see that
> (1-p)^2 * p < (1-p) * p < p and most of the time we expect the associated counts (n001, n01, and n1) to have that same ordering.
>
> For your example n001 = 148, n01 = 22, and n1 = 86.  We see that n1 is much less than n001 which is not expected when visits are independent and have the same detection probability.  This also results in the maximum likelihood estimate of psi being 1.0.
>
> I speculate that anytime n1 is less than or equal to n001, the maximum likelihood estimate for psi will be 1.  Further the estimate of psi will also be 1 whenever n1 isn't much larger than n001.  (I'm going to look into this further to see if there is more specific and justifiable inferences about this.)
>
> All of this suggests that maybe the independence assumption is false or that the probabilities vary by the visit number (or some other deviation from the usual assumptions).
>
> If one considers different probabilities for each visit, then occu will give estimates and a much, much lower AIC value. I clearly don't know if that's a reasonable model for this species (and whoever does the surveying).
>
> Jim

So I next accounted for this in the model (in JAGS, where I find this trivially easy to code up) as follows. Fitting this second model gave very different estimates from the first, mis-specified one and had much better traceplots.
> >

> >     y[i,2] ~ dbern(z[i] * (1 - (1-p)^0.75))   # Second occasion

> >   }

Subject: Seeking Advice on Unmarked for Occupancy Modeling

Dear All,

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I hope this message finds you well.

I am currently working on estimating wild boar abundance in relation to environmental covariates across different study areas using an N-Mixture model. My goal is to compare how an environmental variable influences species abundance across these study areas.

To address this, I was considering adding the study area as a categorical variable in the state process. However, I wanted to ask if it is possible to include an interaction between the study area and environmental covariates in a model using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)?

I hope I have explained the issue clearly, otherwise I will gladly provide more information.

Thanks and best regards,
Luisa

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Interaction Terms in N-Mixture Models possible?
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Interaction Terms in N-Mixture Models possible?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Luisa,

whether one can fit such a model or not has nothing to do with your choice of inference method (i.e., Bayes or non-Bayes). Provided that you have enough data (e.g., enough sites in each study area), you can stratify your abundance (or state) model by study area. In addition, you can specify interactions between covariates and study area, which then simply means to estimate different coefficients in each study area. A comparison of such a model with a model that has no interactions between study area and covariates then tests whether these environmental relationships with abundance are identical across space or not.

However, the one big thing you have to take care of is the big assumption of the Nmix model that you mustn't count the same individual twice within an occasion. Are you sure you can meet this assumption with a species that does not allow individual identification ? (Or does it ? I am no expert on wild boar..).

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vegas,

Another option is to use xtable methods from the AICcmodavg package to
format the output to LaTeX using the xtable package.

Here is an example for an N-mixture model from ?pcount:

library(unmarked)
library(AICcmodavg)
library(xtable) #to export table to LaTeX

##format object
data(mallard)
mallardUMF <- unmarkedFramePCount(mallard.y, siteCovs = mallard.site,
     obsCovs = mallard.obs)
fm.mallard <- pcount(~ ivel+ date + I(date^2) ~ length + elev + forest,
mallardUMF, K=30)

##summary of model
out <- summaryOD(fm.mallard, c.hat = 1)
out

##formatted as LaTeX table
xtable(out)

?summaryOD
?xtable.aictab

Best,

Marc

messages.subject: Trick pcount into fitting a multispecies Nmix model ?
messages.subject_clean: Trick pcount into fitting a multispecies Nmix model ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Ken (*)

some colleagues of mine have been using pcount() to model butterfly counts for about 12 species. They have two back-to-back visits to transects during 3 different periods in a year. Thus, they want to stratify the parameters by period, to account for the often very different abundance at different times during the flight period of a species.

One possibility would be to fit a model with random site effects (to avoid pseudoreplication) plus a fixed period effect. This should be doable in principle in unmarked thanks to the TMB engine.

But, would it also be possible to fit a model to all species at once ? That is, fit an abundance variant of a community occupancy model, as one can now do in unmarked ? Could one specify multiple sets of random effects in pcount such as in (1 | species) + (1 | species:site) ?

Thanks a lot and best regards  --- Marc

(*) sorry if I address you directly, but realistically, nobody else will be able to answer my question. However, I think this question may be of wider interest, so rather than sending you a private mail, I here do it over the list.

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Trick pcount into fitting a multispecies Nmix model ?
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Trick pcount into fitting a multispecies Nmix model ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc,

Yes, this should work. You're already stacking by site, so you're adding another 'stack' by species.

unmarked does not automatically support the species:site notation in the grouping variable of random effects, but you should be able to just create this interaction manually as a new combined factor (species_site) and use it.

The notation gets a bit more complicated once you have covariates. You'd need to do something like

~1 + period + (1 + period | species) + (1|species_site)

to make sure the slopes are appropriately random also.

Initially unmarked did not support automatic handling of factor random slopes (like period) due to the complicated bookkeeping involved. It should work now but definitely would want to double check that you correctly get a separate random slope for each new dummy variable (per2, per3 etc). Alternatively you can just create the dummy variables yourself manually and use them to avoid this.

I'd suggest experimenting with some simulations on the scale of your dataset first. I have found TMB random effects estimation to be a bit less reliable than the equivalent Bayesian model, and I haven't tested pcount enough to know when you might run into trouble.

Ken
